items.title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery
items.summary: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.

items.title: Enhancing Active Learning Performance with Initial Data Selection Based on Foundation Models
items.summary: In active object detection, selecting the initial labeled pool is essential, especially in complex datasets with expensive labeling and low resource budget. This study presents an active learning framework designed to optimize the initial training cycle of active learning for the object detection task. Our approach diverges from traditional methods by utilizing feature-based clustering from the YOLO-World model and refining images based on objectness scores rather than relying on uncertainty sampling in the initial cycle. This approach focuses on finding samples with various features and emphasizes training in areas where the foundation model is most confident. Doing so helps the model better understand different types of objects. For subsequent cycles, we employ a consistency-based sampling technique to maintain the robustness of the training process. To evaluate our method, we use two complex datasets called Aquarium and NWPU VHR-10, which are well known for their diverse object sizes and challenging conditions. In the NWPU dataset, our method increases mAP50 by an average of 6.6% in image-based evaluation. Moreover, the image refinement method shows an improvement of approximately 11% in object-based evaluation. The results show improvements in model performance and labeling time, demonstrating the advantages of using foundation models in early cycles of active learning. An implementation of the algorithm is available at https://github.com/Mhrshd-fllh/ALBoost-FM

items.title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

items.title: SCOUT: Risk-Guided Foundation-Model Escalation for Robust Tissue Detection in Whole-Slide Images
items.summary: Reliable tissue detection is essential for whole-slide image analysis, yet high average segmentation accuracy can conceal failures involving pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining. Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations, but exhaustive inference is computationally demanding and may introduce false-positive tissue predictions. We propose SCOUT (Selective Correction of Uncertain Tissue), a risk-guided cascade that selectively refines an initial thumbnail-based tissue mask. A lightweight audit network estimates the spatial distribution of segmentation errors and prioritizes candidate regions for processing by a frozen pathology foundation model. An asymmetric consensus rule integrates the resulting predictions with the initial mask to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives. A calibrated slide-level review score additionally controls the marginal rate of unflagged case-group failures under the calibration assumptions. Evaluation on a public multi-source, multi-stain benchmark shows that SCOUT reduces the proportion of case groups requiring mask correction from 38.1% for the best released detector to 18.6%, with particularly pronounced improvements in immunohistochemistry. Source-held-out experiments demonstrate better generalization than a segmentation network trained on the same annotations, while selective inference achieves an observed failure rate no higher than processing all candidate regions. Downstream, lymph-node classification with SCOUT masks is non-inferior to that obtained with two of the three released detectors evaluated. A variant built on an openly licensed foundation model is publicly released as an installable Python package with trained weights. These results support risk-guided foundation-model inference as an effective approach to tissue detection across heterogeneous histopathology data.

items.title: CROMPT: Adapting CLIP via Cross-Modal Prompting for Robust Zero-Shot Generalization under Adverse Weather
items.summary: Domain adaptation for semantic segmentation is challenging when target-domain images are unavailable during training. Zero-shot domain adaptation addresses this by adapting models using only textual descriptions of the target domain. items.title: Stabilizing Neural-to-Image Retrieval with Frequency-Domain Priors and Adaptive Supervision
items.summary: Visual neural decoding aims to infer perceived visual stimuli from brain activity, offering important insights into human visual cognition while enabling transformative applications in brain computer interfaces and artificial intelligence. Recent advances in pretrained vision-language models have provided a semantically rich representation space for this task. However, reliable alignment between EEG/MEG signals and visual embeddings remains challenging because neural responses are noisy, highly variable across trials, and subject dependent. To address this issue, we propose a unified neural-to-image retrieval framework that improves retrieval performance by aligning neural and image representations in a shared semantic space. The framework integrates dual-stream adaptation, frequency-domain calibration, and phase-guided temperature modulation to promote more robust cross-modal semantic alignment. Specifically, dual-stream adaptation models a low-dimensional shared subspace with correlation regularization to suppress redundant noise and enhance cross-modal consistency. Frequency-domain calibration conditionally modulates neural representations using amplitude and phase statistics. Phase-guided temperature modulation further adjusts the supervision strength in contrastive learning according to the stability of neural responses. Experiments on THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG under both intra-subject and inter-subject settings demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms strong baselines. These results suggest that robust neural-to-image retrieval under heterogeneous neural conditions benefits from a stable shared semantic space, frequency-informed representation calibration, and adaptive supervision. Code will be released at github.com/wanfkuabc/Geometry-Regularized-Brain-Embeddings.

items.title: PatchAdaNet: Unsupervised class incremental learning using local patches and global adapters
items.summary: Biological learning systems acquire knowledge incrementally through broad, reusable representations established early and kept largely stable, while integrating new experience with minimal interference with previously learned knowledge. Replay-based methods approximate this by storing samples or features from previous tasks and mixing them into the current task. However, memory buffers grow with the number of tasks and may retain task-specific noise that reduces generalization. To address these limitations, we propose PatchAdaNet (Patch Adapter Network), an unsupervised class-incremental learning method for image classification that continually updates feature representations using autoencoders. Since images share structural features such as edges, corners, and shapes, we first divide each image into patches and train independent autoencoders on external data to reconstruct each patch. The layers of all patch encoders are aggregated into global frozen layers that generalize across tasks and remain fixed throughout learning. Learnable adapters then build global image representations from these features to reconstruct the entire image. To prevent feature drift without storing data, we introduce the Global Feature Centroid (GFC), a fixed-size running average of adapter outputs updated after each task to penalizes representation drift. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is applied to the learnable layers to preserve previously learned features by constraining important weights. Finally, a linear classifier is trained on the frozen latent representation and GFC for class-incremental evaluation. We evaluate PatchAdaNet in both CNN and Vision Transformer settings on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet and 5-Datasets, providing a comparative study of the two architectures under identical class-incremental settings. Code is available.

items.title: Assessing Vision-Language Models for Early Prediction of Unsafe Situations in Robotics
items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process visual information and textual instructions and, by using their ability to understand and reason about context, are well-suited for predicting robot failures before they occur. However, evidence supporting this remains limited. To address this, we present an empirical evaluation of VLMs for predicting robot failures. In particular, we experiment with Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision across three robotic case studies (HuRoN, Pal Robotics, and CrowdBot), analyzing both video and odometry data for early failure warning (i.e., before an unsafe situation occurs). Specifically, we evaluate their performance in classifying situations as safe, potentially unsafe, and unsafe, together with uncertainty quantified using various metrics, and study the relationship between uncertainty and performance. Our results showed that Qwen provides the strongest overall classification and prediction-reliability performance, while InternVL shows stronger early-warning capability in several configurations. The results further show that the effect of robot-state information and temporal history depends on the model and evaluation objective. Overall, our findings indicate that general-purpose VLMs can support early robot-safety monitoring, but the most suitable configuration depends on whether the priority is accurate assessment of safety-state, reliable confidence and uncertainty, or timely warning before unsafe events.

items.title: Inherited Adapter Experts for Replay-Free Domain-Incremental Learning
items.summary: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains a model on the same classes in successive domains without keeping earlier images. Per-domain learners freeze a pre-trained ViT and train an additional expert for each new domain: the small set of parameters and the classification head learned on that domain. Test images carry no domain label, so a router selects one expert for each image. Recent work trains this router. However, a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners under 2.7 points of final accuracy relative to always selecting each image's own-domain expert. The experts, not this router, limit accuracy. Our learner, Lamarck, therefore uses this router and strengthens the experts. Its adapters, small trainable layers that correct every image token after each deep ViT block, add 4.4 points of final accuracy on the deepfake benchmark CDDB-Hard. In addition, each expert is initialized from its predecessor at no extra cost: the domains share their classes, so an image misrouted to a later expert loses less. Against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol, Lamarck is first on CDDB-Hard by 5.2 points, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.

items.title: Training Denoising Models of Any Architecture Without Stored Images
items.summary: Can a pretrained denoising model replace the dataset used to train it? We investigate this question through teacher-supervised training, showing for the first time that continuous-time diffusion and flow models of any architecture and size can be trained from random initialization without stored images. Our students regress the teacher's velocity on a rolling pool of noisy samples, advanced along trajectories of random step counts to obtain independent, dense and approximately continuous noise levels. Our method outperforms standard training of the same network on CIFAR-10 for students 4x smaller than the teacher, comes within 0.75 to 1.92 FID of it at the teacher's size and surpasses training on teacher-generated images and step reduction methods without teacher-based initialization. items.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
items.summary: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

items.title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
items.summary: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

items.title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. items.title: Ego2X: Contact-aware Transfer from Egocentric Human Data to Any Robot
items.summary: Embodied models depend on real interaction data, yet collecting it on physical robots is slow and labor-intensive. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines retarget first-person view human videos to robot data via transferring hand and arm motion. They judge fidelity mainly by visual appearance. However, trajectories often fail in terms of physics: fingers hover beside objects, and grippers close on empty space. We argue that how the object moves and the contacts that drive the motion count. Thus, we present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers. Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact on the object by its surface anchor, as well as relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state. Throughout the pipeline, CORE corrects hand-object drift via object-relative constraints, steers inverse kinematics toward contacts the robot must realize, and preserves held objects during arm erasure and robot compositing. On HOT3D, contact-driven correction reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7%, while on EgoDex, contact-driven retargeting realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts, surpassing the official HuRo pipeline (27.9%). In RoboTwin 2.0, post-training X-VLA on Ego2X episodes alone, without simulator demonstrations, raises task success rate from 40.5% zero-shot to 67.0% across 200 paired scenes. We will publicly release our conversion pipeline and CORE-annotated dataset for dexterous hands and parallel grippers.

items.title: Gaussian Primitive Fusion for Any-Resolution Multimodal Images
items.summary: Multimodal image fusion integrates complementary observations from different modalities into a unified representation. Existing methods typically estimate modality contributions on a common discrete grid. When source modalities have different native resolutions, constructing such a grid generally involves resampling, which may introduce artifacts and affect subsequent fusion decisions. To address this problem, we propose Gaussian Primitive Fusion (GPF), which reformulates heterogeneous-resolution fusion in a shared continuous Gaussian space. Instead of first converting source images to a common resolution, GPF directly fits their native-resolution observations with shared Gaussian geometry and modality-specific content representations, and learns modality contributions within the resulting continuous representation. Once optimized, the fused representation is rendered at the finest native resolution without resampling the sources. With heterogeneous-resolution inputs, GPF produces clearer target contours and finer textures, with less blurring and blocking artifacts than resample-then-fuse pipelines. Quantitatively, it achieves the best results on multiple infrared-visible benchmarks against state-of-the-art fusion methods equipped with interpolation or super-resolution frontends.

items.title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
items.summary: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). items.title: Allocentric Memory, Egocentric Acting: A Dual-Frame VLA for Urban Aerial Navigation
items.summary: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. items.title: CommDreamer: Radio-Geometric World Models for Mapless Cellular-Connected UAV Trajectory Planning
items.summary: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. items.title: Target-Consistent Action Guidance via Semi-Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Drifting World Models
items.summary: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.

items.title: Efficient World-Model Planning via Physics-Guided Search Distillation
items.summary: World models support autonomous driving by evaluating candidate trajectories through predicted future scene evolution. However, accurate future prediction does not ensure road-compliant execution; when all candidates violate road boundaries, re-ranking cannot select a feasible trajectory. We propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), a single-view planning framework that combines future representations and execution feedback for verified beyond-pool repair through three components: (1) Execution-Aware Selection checks ego-vehicle road compliance under simulated execution and selects the highest-scoring feasible trajectory; (2) a Clearance-Aware Search Teacher generates beyond-pool corrections and selects demonstrations with larger minimum road-boundary clearance during execution to buffer imitation errors; and (3) a Future-Conditioned Repair Student predicts one correction from rewarder features and execution feedback for single-rollout verification. The pretrained planner and rewarder remain frozen; no future scenes are generated online. On NAVSIM v1, single-view PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS, exceeding all compared prior single-view planners and retaining 73.2% of the search teacher's PDMS gain over execution-aware selection. On NAVSIM v2 navhard, it reaches 38.96 EPDMS, improving on WorldDrive by 11.24 points (40.5%). The student replaces up to ten search rollouts with a single verification rollout per repair trigger. HUGSIM Hard examples provide qualitative evidence of zero-shot transfer.

items.title: IDEA: Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit for Inference-Time Backdoor Detection in GUI Agents
items.summary: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps, the instruction drives the action; when an unreferenced screen region hijacks the step, the instruction loses control over the decision state or that region dictates it instead. We term this signature intent--evidence dominance inversion and propose IDEA (Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit) to detect backdoor activation at inference time for each step without trigger knowledge or attack data. Specifically, Intent Counterfactual Probing (ICP) measures how far redirected instructions move the decision state, and Region Causal Audit (RCA) quantifies how far ablating a candidate region moves it. A gated conformal score compares both displacements against clean steps at the same distance from the clean manifold, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families show that IDEA consistently detects backdoor activation under a controlled false-positive rate and outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods, while localizing the trigger region for every alarm and adding only modest inference overhead.

items.title: Where Should a Diffusion Transformer Meet Its Teacher?
items.summary: Representation Alignment (REPA) significantly accelerates Diffusion Transformer training by guiding intermediate student features with a pretrained visual teacher, yet existing methods typically attach supervision to a single fixed layer. This probabilistic routing adapts teacher supervision to the student's changing learning needs, with minimal training overhead and no additional inference cost. On ImageNet-256, AdaREPA accelerates convergence and improves generation quality across model sizes, while revealing how the most suitable layers for supervision shift over training.

items.title: Look Closer, Look Back, or Wait for Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
items.summary: Streaming video models must answer questions about a live video under strict memory and latency limits. Feeding only the latest few frames keeps present perception sharp, whereas adding past frames dilutes attention on the current scene and triggers hallucinations. Recent cascade methods retrieve past frames when uncertain, but they still fail when current frames are blurry or when decisive future clues have not appeared yet. We introduce ActiveForager, a streaming video agent that maintains a clean short working window and gathers extra evidence only on demand. For each query, the agent either answers directly, zooms into high-resolution recent frames, recalls past events from memory, or waits for upcoming frames. When recalling history, a shared-weight sub-agent verifies candidate clips in isolation and returns a compact evidence summary. A stream-decoupled attention mask then keeps historical evidence from interfering with present visual tokens. We train this policy using counterfactual information gain, which rewards a tool call only when the gathered evidence makes the true answer more likely and prevents tool collapse across all actions. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on OVO-Bench, ActiveForager improves real-time perception, historical recall, and proactive response at once, lifting overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9%. It also doubles zero-shot accuracy on the multi-hop Video-Holmes benchmark while adding minimal visual tokens per query.

items.title: Old Experience, New Lessons: Relabeling Autonomous Robot Rollouts in Interactive Imitation Learning
items.summary: Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels. Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets. A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to improve policy performance.

items.title: Teaching VLMs What to Say, Not How to Reason: Rethinking Counterfactual Reasoning in Autonomous Driving
items.summary: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have been shown to suffer from shortcut learning and causal confusion, limiting their ability to generalize robustly under distribution shift. To mitigate these limitations, recent works based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored incorporating linguistic reasoning capabilities into driving decision-making, reporting improvements in driving performance. In particular, counterfactual (CF) reasoning has been proposed to enable self-reflective, high-level causal understanding. However, it remains unclear whether the language-based reasoning mitigates shortcut learning or merely shifts it from visual representations to linguistic patterns, creating an illusion of causal understanding. Moreover, existing approaches often conflate intervention-based reasoning with CF reasoning, leaving the effects of genuine CF reasoning unexplored. In this work, we examine what CF reasoning actually induces in VLM-based autonomous driving and observe that it shifts the action distribution toward more conservative behaviors while increasing uncertainty in reasoning and decision-making. This effect persists under reinforcement fine-tuning, suggesting that it is not merely a transient artifact. Furthermore, visual attention analysis shows that CF reasoning does not alter visual grounding, while causal intervention experiments reveal that masking causally relevant and non-causal factors in accident scenarios results in comparable decision change rates. Overall, these results suggest that CF reasoning does not induce genuine causal reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Instead, it acts as a linguistic shortcut that reshapes the action distribution, teaching models what to say but not how to reason, highlighting a gap between language-based reasoning and causal understanding in autonomous driving.

items.title: AnchorUp: Anchoring Feature Upsampling on a Classical Interpolation
items.summary: Vision foundation models produce semantically strong features on a coarse patch grid, and dense prediction needs them at pixel resolution. Existing learned upsamplers close that gap by regressing the high-resolution feature map from the low-resolution one, typically through cross-attention driven by the input image. We observe that most of what they regress needs no learning: plain bilinear interpolation already reproduces the smooth regions of the target, and recent benchmarks even report bilinear and bicubic on par with several learned upsamplers. The rest is mostly edges and fine details, which suggests that these learned upsamplers spend much of their capacity re-computing the smooth content that classical interpolation provides. We therefore introduce AnchorUp, which stops predicting the high-resolution feature map and predicts only its correction from the interpolation. It keeps a parameter-free classical upsampler as an anchor, obtains a second prediction from a small guidance network, and blends the two through a single learnable scalar gate. Because the anchor supplies the smooth content, the guidance network only has to correct what remains. An analysis of the learned correction confirms that it concentrates on edges and fine details, and so the network can be small: AnchorUp uses 167,425 parameters, a quarter of the budget of the strongest baseline, NAF, and runs at 64% of its latency. Trained once on DINOv3 with only the first of NAF's two training stages, and evaluated on that backbone plus six held-out ones, it is already on par with NAF trained through both stages on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes. Our method surpasses it on DAVIS-2017 video object segmentation; the gain holds on every backbone and is larger in contour accuracy F. Code is available at https://github.com/KotaroHorikawa/AnchorUp.

items.title: Dual-Actuation Emulation of Scaled Relative Orbital Dynamics on a Free-Flyer
items.summary: Ground-based free-flyer testbeds reproduce the planar motion of a free-floating spacecraft using air bearings, but not the relative dynamics of spacecraft in orbit. items.title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
items.summary: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. items.title: Do Thinking VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away
items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

items.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
items.summary: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. items.title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
items.summary: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

items.title: GenRF: Generative Registration-free Image Fusion
items.summary: Multi-modal image fusion combines complementary observations to improve scene visibility and perception. However, in real-world acquisition, differences in sensing principles and configurations introduce geometric discrepancies, while degradations further compromise source quality. Existing methods typically rely on explicit registration, yet large parallax complicates correspondence estimation, while mismatched fields of view leave some regions without cross-modal counterparts. Meanwhile, independent restoration underuses cross-modal information, whereas restoration-fusion methods assuming alignment remain vulnerable to misregistration. This study revisits misaligned and degraded image fusion in the era of generative foundation models, in which cross-attention enables position-agnostic complementary information aggregation, while generative priors support degradation recovery and inference in missing regions. Building on this perspective, we propose GenRF, which adapts pretrained FLUX through LoRA to jointly enhance degraded observations, infer missing cross-modal context, and fuse complementary information without explicitly estimating deformation fields. Extensive experiments on real-world infrared and visible captures show that GenRF delivers high-quality fusion directly from unregistered, degraded images without preprocessing, while improving downstream task performance under misalignment. Additional experiments demonstrate that GenRF can generalize to misaligned multi-exposure and multi-focus image fusion without task-specific fine-tuning. items.title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

items.title: Gradient-based Planning for World Models at Longer Horizons
items.summary:
GRASP is a new gradient-based planner for learned dynamics (a "world model") that makes long-horizon planning practical by (1) lifting the trajectory into virtual states so optimization is parallel across time, (2) adding stochasticity directly to the state iterates for exploration, and (3) reshaping gradients so actions get clean signals while we avoid brittle "state-input" gradients through high-dimensional vision models. Large, learned world models are becoming increasingly capable. They can predict long sequences of future observations in high-dimensional visual spaces and generalize across tasks in ways that were difficult to imagine a few years ago. As these models scale, they start to look less like task-specific predictors and more like general-purpose simulators. But having a powerful predictive model is not the same as being able to use it effectively for control/learning/planning. In practice, long-horizon planning with modern world models remains fragile: optimization becomes ill-conditioned, non-greedy structure creates bad local minima, and high-dimensional latent spaces introduce subtle failure modes. In this blog post, I describe the problems that motivated this project and our approach to address them: why planning with modern world models can be surprisingly fragile, why long horizons are the real stress test, and what we changed to make gradient-based planning much more robust. This blog post discusses work done with Mike Rabbat, Aditi Krishnapriyan, Yann LeCun, and Amir Bar (* denotes equal advisorship), where we propose GRASP. What is a world model? These days, the term "world model" is quite overloaded, and depending on the context can either mean an explicit dynamics model or some implicit, reliable internal state that a generative model relies on (e.g. when an LLM generates chess moves, whether there is some internal representation of the board). We give our loose working definition below. Suppose you take actions $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$ and observe states $s_t \in \mathcal{S}$ (images, latent vectors, proprioception). A world model is a learned model that, given the current state and a sequence of future actions, predicts what will happen next. Formally, it defines a predictive distribution on a sequence of observed states $s_{t-h:t}$ and current action $a_t$: \[P_	heta(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)\] that approximates the environment's true conditional $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)$. For this blog post, we'll assume a Markovian model $P(s_{t+1} \mid s_{t-h:t},\; a_t)$ for simplicity (all results here can be extended to the more general case), and when the model is deterministic it reduces to a map over states: \[s_{t+1} = F_	heta(s_t, a_t).\] In practice the state $s_t$ is often a learned latent representation (e.g., encoded from pixels), so the model operates in a (theoretically) compact, differentiable space. The key point is that a world model gives you a differentiable simulator ; you can roll it forward under hypothetical action sequences and backpropagate through the predictions. Planning: choosing actions by optimizing through the model Given a start $s_0$ and a goal $g$, the simplest planner chooses an action sequence $\mathbf{a}=(a_0,\dots,a_{T-1})$ by rolling out the model and minimizing terminal error: \[\min_{\mathbf{a}} \; \| s_T(\mathbf{a}) - g \|_2^2, \quad 	ext{where } s_T(\mathbf{a}) = \mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0,\mathbf{a}).\] Here we use $\mathcal{F}^T$ as shorthand for the full rollout through the world model (dependence on model parameters $	heta$ is implicit): \[\mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0, \mathbf{a}) = F_	heta(F_	heta(\cdots F_	heta(s_0, a_0), \cdots, a_{T-2}), a_{T-1}).\] In short horizons and low-dimensional systems, this can work reasonably well. But as horizons grow and models become larger and more expressive, its weaknesses become amplified. So why doesn't this just work at scale? Why long-horizon planning is hard (even when everything is differentiable) There are two separate pain points for the more general world model, plus a third that is specific to learned, deep learning-based models. 1) Long-horizon rollouts create deep, ill-conditioned computation graphs Those familiar with backprop through time (BPTT) may notice that we're differentiating through a model applied to itself repeatedly, which will lead to the exploding/vanishing gradients problem. Namely, if we take derivatives (note we're differentiating vector-valued functions, resulting in Jacobians that we denote with $D_x (\cdots)$) with respect to earlier actions (e.g. $a_0$): \[D_{a_0} \mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}(s_0, \mathbf{a}) = \Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^T D_s F_	heta(s_t, a_t)\Bigr) D_{a_0}F_	heta(s_0, a_0).\] We see that the Jacobian's conditioning scales exponentially with time $T$: \[\sigma_{	ext{max/min}}(D_{a_0}\mathcal{F}_{	heta}^{T}) \sim \sigma_{	ext{max/min}}(D_s F_	heta)^{T-1},\] leading to exploding or vanishing gradients. 2) The landscape is non-greedy and full of traps At short horizons, the greedy solution, where we move straight toward the goal at every step, is often good enough. If you only need to plan a few steps ahead, the optimal trajectory usually doesn't deviate much from "head toward $g$" at each step. As horizons grow, two things happen. First, longer tasks are more likely to require non-greedy behavior: going around a wall, repositioning before pushing, backing up to take a better path. And as horizons grow, more of these non-greedy steps are typically needed. Second, the optimization space itself scales with horizon: $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A} 	imes \cdots 	imes \mathcal{A}) = T\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A})$, further expanding the space of local minima for the optimization problem. Distance to goal along the optimal path is non-monotonic, and the resulting loss landscape can be rough. A long-horizon fix: lifting the dynamics constraint Suppose we treat the dynamics constraint $s_{t+1} = F_{	heta}(s_t, a_t)$ as a soft constraint, and we instead optimize the following penalty function over both actions $(a_0,\ldots,a_{T-1})$ and states $(s_0,\ldots,s_T)$: \[\min_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2, \quad 	ext{with } s_0 	ext{ fixed and } s_T=g.\] This is also sometimes called collocation in planning/robotics literature. Note the lifted formulation shares the same global minimizers as the original rollout objective (both are zero exactly when the trajectory is dynamically feasible). But the optimization landscapes are very different, and we get two immediate benefits: Each world model evaluation $F_{	heta}(s_t,a_t)$ depends only on local variables, so all $T$ terms can be computed in parallel across time , resulting in a huge speed-up for longer horizons, and You no longer backpropagate through a single deep $T$-step composition to get a learning signal, since the previous product of Jacobians now splits into a sum, e.g.: \[D_{a_0} \mathcal{L} = 2(F_	heta(s_0, a_0) - s_1).\] Being able to optimize states directly also helps with exploration, as we can temporarily navigate through unphysical domains to find the optimal plan: Collocation-based planning allows us to directly perturb states and explore midpoints more effectively. However, lunch is never free. And indeed, especially for deep learning-based world models, there is a critical issue that makes the above optimization quite difficult in practice. An issue for deep learning-based world models: sensitivity of state-input gradients The tl;dr of this section is: directly optimizing states through a deep learning-based $F_{	heta}$ is incredibly brittle, à la adversarial robustness . Even if you train your world model in a lower-dimensional state space, the training process for the world model makes unseen state landscapes very sharp, whether it be an unseen state itself or simply a normal/orthogonal direction to the data manifold. Adversarial robustness and the "dimpled manifold" model Adversarial robustness originally looked at classification models $f_	heta : \mathbb{R}^{w	imes h 	imes c} 	o \mathbb{R}^K$, and showed that by following the gradient of a particular logit $
abla f_	heta^k$ from a base image $x$ (not of class $k$), you did not have to move far along $x' = x + \epsilon
abla f_	heta^k$ to make $f_	heta$ classify $x'$ as $k$ ( Szegedy et al., 2014 ; Goodfellow et al., 2015 ): Depiction of the classic example from (Goodfellow et al., 2015). Later work has painted a geometric picture for what's going on: for data near a low-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$, the training process controls behavior in tangential directions, but does not regularize behavior in orthogonal directions, thus leading to sensitive behavior ( Stutz et al., 2019 ). Another way stated: $f_	heta$ has a reasonable Lipschitz constant when considering only tangential directions to the data manifold $\mathcal{M}$, but can have very high Lipschitz constants in normal directions. In fact, it often benefits the model to be sharper in these normal directions, so it can fit more complicated functions more precisely. As a result, such adversarial examples are incredibly common even for a single given model. Further, this is not just a computer vision phenomenon; adversarial examples also appear in LLMs ( Wallace et al., 2019 ) and in RL ( Gleave et al., 2019 ). While there are methods to train for more adversarially robust models, there is a known trade-off between model performance and adversarial robustness ( Tsipras et al., 2019 ): especially in the presence of many weakly-correlated variables, the model must be sharper to achieve higher performance. Indeed, most modern training algorithms, whether in computer vision or LLMs, do not train adversarial robustness out. Thus, at least until deep learning sees a major regime change, this is a problem we're stuck with . Why is adversarial robustness an issue for world model planning? Consider a single component of the dynamics loss we're optimizing in the lifted state approach: \[\min_{s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}} \|F_	heta(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}\|_2^2\] Let's further focus on just the base state: \[\min_{s_t} \|F_	heta(s_t, a_t) - s_{t+1}\|_2^2.\] Since world models are typically trained on state/action trajectories $(s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, \ldots)$, the state-data manifold for $F_{	heta}$ has dimensionality bounded by the action space: \[\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{M}_s) \le \mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{A}) + 1 + \mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{R}),\] where $\mathcal{R}$ is some optional space of augmentations (e.g. translations/rotations). Thus, we can typically expect $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{M}_s)$ to be much lower than $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{S})$, and thus: it is very easy to find adversarial examples that hack any state to any other desired state. As a result, the dynamics optimization \[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2\] feels incredibly "sticky," as the base points $s_t$ can easily trick $F_{	heta}$ into thinking it's already made its local goal. 1 1. This adversarial robustness issue, while particularly bad for lifted-state approaches, is not unique to them. Even for serial optimization methods that optimize through the full rollout map $\mathcal{F}^T$, it is possible to get into unseen states, where it is very easy to have a normal component fed into the sensitive normal components of $D_s F_{	heta}$. The action Jacobian's chain rule expansion is \[\Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^T D_s F_	heta(s_t, a_t)\Bigr) D_{a_0}F_	heta(s_0, a_0).\] See what happens if any stage of the product has any component normal to the data manifold. ↩ Our fix This is where our new planner GRASP comes in. The main observation: while $D_s F_{	heta}$ is untrustworthy and adversarial, the action space is usually low-dimensional and exhaustively trained, so $D_a F_{	heta}$ is actually reasonable to optimize through and doesn't suffer from the adversarial robustness issue! The action input is usually lower-dimensional and densely trained (the model has seen every action direction), so action gradients are much better behaved. At its core, GRASP builds a first-order lifted state / collocation-based planner that is only dependent on action Jacobians through the world model. We thus exploit the differentiability of learned world models $F_{	heta}$, while not falling victim to the inherent sensitivity of the state Jacobians $D_s F_{	heta}$. GRASP: Gradient RelAxed S tochastic P lanner As noted before, we start with the collocation planning objective, where we lift the states and relax dynamics into a penalty: \[\min_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta(s_t,a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2, \quad 	ext{with } s_0 	ext{ fixed and } s_T=g.\] We then make two key additions. Ingredient 1: Exploration by noising the state iterates Even with a smoother objective, planning is nonconvex. We introduce exploration by injecting Gaussian noise into the virtual state updates during optimization. A simple version: \[s_t \leftarrow s_t - \eta_s 
abla_{s_t}\mathcal{L} + \sigma_{	ext{state}} \xi, \qquad \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I).\] Actions are still updated by non-stochastic descent: \[a_t \leftarrow a_t - \eta_a 
abla_{a_t}\mathcal{L}.\] The state noise helps you "hop" between basins in the lifted space, while the actions remain guided by gradients. We found that specifically noising states here (as opposed to actions) finds a good balance of exploration and the ability to find sharper minima. 2 2. Because we only noise the states (and not the actions), the corresponding dynamics are not truly Langevin dynamics. ↩ Ingredient 2: Reshape gradients: stop brittle state-input gradients, keep action gradients As discussed, the fragile pathway is the gradient that flows into the state input of the world model, \(D_s F_{	heta}\) . The most straightforward way to do this initially is to just stop state gradients into \(F_{	heta}\) directly: Let $ ar{s}_t$ be the same value as $s_t$, but with gradients stopped. Define the stop-gradient dynamics loss : \[\mathcal{L}_{	ext{dyn}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta( ar{s}_t, a_t) - s_{t+1} ig\|_2^2.\] This alone does not work. Notice now states only follow the previous state's step, without anything forcing the base states to chase the next ones. As a result, there are trivial minima for just stopping at the origin, then only for the final action trying to get to the goal in one step. Dense goal shaping We can view the above issue as the goal's signal being cut off entirely from previous states. One way to fix this is to simply add a dense goal term throughout prediction: \[\mathcal{L}_{	ext{goal}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}  ig\|F_	heta( ar{s}_t, a_t) - g ig\|_2^2.\] In normal settings this would over-bias towards the greedy solution of straight chasing the goal, but this is balanced in our setting by the stop-gradient dynamics loss's bias towards feasible dynamics. The final objective is then as follows: \[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) = \mathcal{L}_{	ext{dyn}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}) + \gamma \, \mathcal{L}_{	ext{goal}}^{	ext{sg}}(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{a}).\] The result is a planning optimization objective that does not have dependence on state gradients. Periodic "sync": briefly return to true rollout gradients The lifted stop-gradient objective is great for fast, guided exploration , but it's still an approximation of the original serial rollout objective. So every $K_{	ext{sync}}$ iterations, GRASP does a short refinement phase: Roll out from $s_0$ using current actions $\mathbf{a}$, and take a few small gradient steps on the original serial loss: \[\mathbf{a} \leftarrow \mathbf{a} - \eta_{	ext{sync}}\,
abla_{\mathbf{a}}\,\|s_T(\mathbf{a})-g\|_2^2.\] The lifted-state optimization still provides the core of the optimization, while this refinement step adds some assistance to keep states and actions grounded towards real trajectories. This refinement step can of course be replaced with a serial planner of your choice (e.g. CEM); the core idea is to still get some of the benefit of the full-path synchronization of serial planners, while still mostly using the benefits of the lifted-state planning. How GRASP addresses long-range planning Collocation-based planners offer a natural fix for long-horizon planning, but this optimization is quite difficult through modern world models due to adversarial robustness issues. GRASP proposes a simple solution for a smoother collocation-based planner, alongside stable stochasticity for exploration . As a result, longer-horizon planning ends up not only succeeding more, but also finding such successes faster: Push-T demo: longer-horizon planning with GRASP. Horizon CEM GD LatCo GRASP H=40 61.4% / 35.3s 51.0% / 18.0s 15.0% / 598.0s 59.0% / 8.5s H=50 30.2% / 96.2s 37.6% / 76.3s 4.2% / 1114.7s 43.4% / 15.2s H=60 7.2% / 83.1s 16.4% / 146.5s 2.0% / 231.5s 26.2% / 49.1s H=70 7.8% / 156.1s 12.0% / 103.1s 0.0% / — 16.0% / 79.9s H=80 2.8% / 132.2s 6.4% / 161.3s 0.0% / — 10.4% / 58.9s Push-T results. Success rate (%) / median time to success. Bold = best in row. Note the median success time will bias higher with higher success rate; GRASP manages to be faster despite higher success rate. What's next? There is still plenty of work to be done for modern world model planners. We want to exploit the gradient structure of learned world models, and collocation (lifted-state optimization) is a natural approach for long-horizon planning, but it's crucial to understand typical gradient structure here: smooth and informative action gradients and brittle state gradients. We view GRASP as an initial iteration for such planners. Extension to diffusion-based world models (deeper latent timesteps can be viewed as smoothed versions of the world model itself), more sophisticated optimizers and noising strategies, and integrating GRASP into either a closed-loop system or RL policy learning for adaptive long-horizon planning are all natural and interesting next steps. I do genuinely think it's an exciting time to be working on world model planners. It's a funny sweet spot where the background literature (planning and control overall) is incredibly mature and well-developed, but the current setting (pure planning optimization over modern, large-scale world models) is still heavily underexplored. But, once we figure out all the right ideas, world model planners will likely become as commonplace as RL. For more details, read the full paper or visit the project website . items.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
items.summary: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.

items.title: Monitoring Unplanned Construction Using Satellite Change Detection
items.summary: Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. We feed those numbers to standard machine-learning classifiers that predict land categories and physical changes. The methods reach about 95 percent accuracy at spotting built-up land and about 83 percent accuracy at saying whether a small pair of images shows change, where each pair gets one label. We also train a small neural network on a standard change-detection benchmark. Separately, we run a preliminary descriptive check on an Agra sample of 48 patches, 7 of them positive. The results show that satellite images carry information about physical change. They do not show whether construction was planned or permitted.

items.title: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination
items.summary: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.

items.title: SEER: Semantic Evidence for Executable Region Propagation in Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
items.summary: Training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has made strong progress by adapting CLIP-like representations to dense prediction, but its remaining errors are often local, structured, and tied to the active label space. A successful correction must be visually plausible, legal under the target vocabulary, and executable in the segmentation score field. We propose SEER, a training-free test-time repair layer for Semantic Evidence and Executable Region propagation. SEER casts post-prediction OVSS repair as evidence-conditioned label propagation. The OVSS score space proposes compact candidate labels, a frozen VLM verifies closed-set regional evidence, and an execution gate certifies whether the evidence is legally and semantically actionable. The accepted label is then propagated by an OVSS-side policy: coherent high-confidence regions allow broad propagation, while object- or boundary-risk cases use conservative score-grounded propagation. Across eight standard OVSS benchmarks, SEER reaches 58.0 average mIoU without updating OVSS weights. Matched-input controls isolate the repair mechanism, while resource measurements report the cost of the complete frozen system.

items.title: This robot helps you lift objects — by looking at your biceps
items.summary: This robot helps you lift objects — by looking at your biceps rachelg Wed, 05/22/2019 - 10:30 Video May 22 '19 Rachel Gordon CSAIL system can mirror a user's motions and follow nonverbal commands by monitoring arm muscles. We humans are very good at collaboration. For instance, when two people work together to carry a heavy object like a table or a sofa, they tend to instinctively coordinate their motions, constantly recalibrating to make sure their hands are at the same height as the other person's. Our natural ability to make these types of adjustments allows us to collaborate on tasks big and small. But a computer or a robot still can't follow a human's lead with ease. We usually either explicitly program them using machine-speak, or train them to understand our words, à la virtual assistants like Siri or Alexa. In contrast, researchers at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) recently showed that a smoother robot-human collaboration is possible through a new system they developed, where machines help people lift objects by monitoring their muscle movements. Dubbed RoboRaise, the system involves putting electromyography (EMG) sensors on a user's biceps and triceps to monitor muscle activity. Its algorithms then continuously detect changes to the person's arm level, as well as discrete up-and-down hand gestures the user might make for finer motor control. The team used the system for a series of tasks involving picking up and assembling mock airplane components. In experiments, users worked on these tasks with the robot and were able to control it to within a few inches of the desired heights by lifting and then tensing their arm. It was more accurate when gestures were used, and the robot responded correctly to roughly 70 percent of all gestures. Graduate student Joseph DelPreto says he could imagine people using RoboRaise to help in manufacturing and construction settings, or even as an assistant around the house. "Our approach to lifting objects with a robot aims to be intuitive and similar to how you might lift something with another person — roughly copying each other's motions while inferring helpful adjustments," says DelPreto, lead author on a new paper about the project with MIT Professor and CSAIL Director Daniela Rus. "The key insight is to use nonverbal cues that encode instructions for how to coordinate, for example to lift a little higher or lower. Using muscle signals to communicate almost makes the robot an extension of yourself that you can fluidly control." The project builds off the team's existing system that allows users to instantly correct robot mistakes with brainwaves and hand gestures, now enabling continuous motion in a more collaborative way. "We aim to develop human-robot interaction where the robot adapts to the human, rather than the other way around. This way the robot becomes an intelligent tool for physical work," says Rus. EMG signals can be tricky to work with: They're often very noisy, and it can be difficult to predict exactly how a limb is moving based on muscle activity. Even if you can estimate how a person is moving, how you want the robot itself to respond may be unclear. RoboRaise gets around this by putting the human in control. The team's system uses noninvasive, on-body sensors that detect the firing of neurons as you tense or relax muscles. Using wearables also gets around problems of occlusions or ambient noise, which can complicate tasks involving vision or speech. RoboRaise's algorithm then processes biceps activity to estimate how the person's arm is moving so the robot can roughly mimic it, and the person can slightly tense or relax their arm to move the robot up or down. If a user needs the robot to move farther away from their own position or hold a pose for a while, they can just gesture up or down for finer control; a neural network detects these gestures at any time based on biceps and triceps activity. A new user can start using the system very quickly, with minimal calibration. After putting on the sensors, they just need to tense and relax their arm a few times then lift a light weight to a few heights. The neural network that detects gestures is only trained on data from previous users. The team tested the system with 10 users through a series of three lifting experiments: one where the robot didn't move at all, another where the robot moved in response to their muscles but didn't help lift the object, and a third where the robot and person lifted an object together. When the person had feedback from the robot — when they could see it moving or when they were lifting something together — the achieved height was significantly more accurate compared to having no feedback. The team also tested RoboRaise on assembly tasks, such as lifting a rubber sheet onto a base structure. It was able to successfully lift both rigid and flexible objects onto the bases. RoboRaise was implemented on the team's Baxter humanoid robot, but the team says it could be adapted for any robotic platform. items.title: SearchDiffusion: Information-Guided Diffusion Planning for Object Search
items.summary: Object search in unknown environments requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles and accounting for limited sensor visibility. We present SearchDiffusion, a diffusion-based planner that generates position and heading trajectories using a learned dense utility map. The map represents geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress. It conditions trajectory generation and provides an objective for sampling guidance. Sampled map hypotheses provide additional geometric context, while geometric and heading guidance, validity checks, and analytical selection support execution. Across 90 simulated tasks on 24 map layouts, SearchDiffusion achieved 95.6\% target detection at greater computational cost. Ablations show complementary benefits from utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime map hypotheses. In ten physical quadruped trials using OneMap relevance maps, eight were successful under operator assessment, without fine-tuning on real-robot data. These results support combining learned spatial utility with guided trajectory generation for object search under partial observability.

items.title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
items.summary: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.

items.title: Psychometrics-Inspired Coreset Selection for Image Quality Assessment
items.summary: Collecting large-scale subjective annotations remains a critical bottleneck in training accurate image quality assessment (IQA) models. Coreset selection reduces this burden by selecting representative images before annotation. However, diversity in a visual feature space does not necessarily reflect diversity in perceptual quality, raising a fundamental question about which quality-related factors the representation should encode. We propose GRAM, a quality-aware representation learning framework inspired by the graded response model (GRM) from psychometrics. GRM describes how an individual's latent ability determines the probabilities of reaching successive assessment grades, with response sensitivity and grade thresholds governing this relationship. In this paper, we find that this principle naturally aligns with perceptual quality assessment, where the impact of image degradation depends on image content and distortion characteristics. Building on this connection, GRAM models quality judgments through three complementary factors: latent quality, content-dependent response sensitivity, and distortion-dependent grade thresholds. These factors jointly determine the probabilities of attaining different quality grades and the resulting expected quality score. The learned parameters provide a structured quality-aware representation that complements general visual features for coreset selection. Experiments on nine datasets demonstrate improvements across different selection strategies, downstream IQA models, and annotation budgets. The code will be made publicly available.
