items.title: Adaptive Parallel Reasoning: The Next Paradigm in Efficient Inference Scaling
items.summary: Overview of adaptive parallel reasoning. What if a reasoning model could decide for itself when to decompose and parallelize independent subtasks, how many concurrent threads to spawn, and how to coordinate them based on the problem at hand? We provide a detailed analysis of recent progress in the field of parallel reasoning, especially Adaptive Parallel Reasoning. Disclosure: this post is part landscape survey, part perspective on adaptive parallel reasoning. One of the authors (Tony Lian) co-led ThreadWeaver ( Lian et al., 2025 ), one of the methods discussed below. The authors aim to present each approach on its own terms. Motivation Recent progress in LLM reasoning capabilities has been largely driven by inference-time scaling, in addition to data and parameter scaling ( OpenAI et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ). Models that explicitly output reasoning tokens (through intermediate steps, backtracking, and exploration) now dominate math, coding, and agentic benchmarks. These behaviors allow models to explore alternative hypotheses, correct earlier mistakes, and synthesize conclusions rather than committing to a single solution ( Wen et al., 2025 ). The problem is that sequential reasoning scales linearly with the amount of exploration. Scaling sequential reasoning tokens comes at a cost, as models risk exceeding effective context limits ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ). The accumulation of intermediate exploration paths makes it challenging for the model to disambiguate amongst distractors when attending to information in its context, leading to a degradation of model performance, also known as context-rot ( Hong, Troynikov and Huber, 2025 ). Latency also grows proportionally with reasoning length. For complex tasks requiring millions of tokens for exploration and planning, it's not uncommon to see users wait tens of minutes or even hours for an answer ( Qu et al., 2025 ). As we continue to scale along the output sequence length dimension, we also make inference slower, less reliable, and more compute-intensive. Parallel reasoning has emerged as a natural solution. Instead of exploring paths sequentially ( Gandhi et al., 2024 ) and accumulating the context window at every step, we can allow models to explore multiple threads independently (threads don't rely on each other's context) and concurrently (threads can be executed at the same time). Figure 1: Sequential vs. Parallel Reasoning Over recent years, a growing body of work has explored this idea across synthetic settings (e.g., the Countdown game ( Katz, Kokel and Sreedharan, 2025 )), real-world math problems, and general reasoning tasks. From Fixed Parallelism to Adaptive Control Existing approaches show that parallel reasoning can help, but most of them still decide the parallel structure outside the model rather than letting the model choose it. Simple fork-and-join. Self-consistency/Majority Voting — independently sample multiple complete reasoning traces, extract final answer from each, and return the most common one ( Wang et al., 2023 ). Best-of-N (BoN) — similar to self-consistency, but uses a trained verifier to select the best solution instead of using majority voting ( Stiennon et al., 2022 ). Although simple to implement, these methods often incur redundant computation across branches since trajectories are sampled independently. Heuristic-based structured search. Tree / Graph / Skeleton of Thoughts — a family of structured decomposition methods that explores multiple alternative "thoughts" using known search algorithms (BFS/DFS) and prunes via LLM-based evaluation ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Besta et al., 2024 ; Ning et al., 2024 ). Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) — estimates node values by sampling random rollouts and expands the search tree with Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) style exploration-exploitation ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ). These methods improve upon simple fork-and-join by decomposing tasks into non-overlapping subtasks; however, they require prior knowledge about the decomposition strategy, which is not always known. Recent variants. ParaThinker — trains a model to run in two fixed stages: first generating multiple reasoning threads in parallel, then synthesizing them. They introduce trainable control tokens ( <think_i> ) and thought-specific positional embeddings to enforce independence during reasoning and controlled integration during summarization via a two-phase attention mask ( Wen et al., 2025 ). GroupThink — multiple parallel reasoning threads can see each other's partial progress at token level and adapt mid-generation. Unlike prior concurrent methods that operate on independent requests, GroupThink runs a single LLM producing multiple interdependent reasoning trajectories simultaneously ( Hsu et al., 2025 ). Hogwild! Inference — multiple parallel reasoning threads share KV cache and decide how to decompose tasks without an explicit coordination protocol. Workers generate concurrently into a shared attention cache using RoPE to stitch together individual KV blocks in different orders without recomputation ( Rodionov et al., 2025 ). Figure 2: Various Strategies for Parallel Reasoning The methods above share a common limitation: the decision to parallelize, the level of parallelization, and the search strategy are imposed on the model, regardless of whether the problem actually benefits from it. However, different problems need different levels of parallelization, and that is something critical to the effectiveness of parallelization. For example, a framework that applies the same parallel structure to "What's 25+42?" and "What's the smallest planar region in which you can continuously rotate a unit-length line segment by 180°?" is wasting compute on the former and probably using the wrong decomposition strategy for the latter. In the approaches described above, the model is not taught this adaptive behavior. A natural question arises: What if the model could decide for itself when to parallelize, how many threads to spawn, and how to coordinate them based on the problem at hand? Adaptive Parallel Reasoning (APR) answers this question by making parallelization part of the model's generated control flow. Formally defined, adaptivity refers to the model's ability to dynamically allocate compute between parallel and serial operations at inference time . In other words, a model with adaptive parallel reasoning (APR) capability is taught to coordinate its control flow — when to generate sequences sequentially vs. in parallel. It's important to note that the concept of adaptive parallel reasoning was introduced by the work Learning Adaptive Parallel Reasoning with Language Models ( Pan et al., 2025 ), but is a paradigm rather than a specific method. Throughout this post, APR refers to the paradigm, while " the APR method " denotes the specific instantiation from Pan et al. (2025). This shift matters for three reasons. Compared to Tree-of-Thoughts, APR doesn't need domain-specific heuristics for decomposition. During RL, the model learns general decomposition strategies from trial and error. In fact, models discover useful parallelization patterns, such as running the next step along with the self-verification of a previous step, or hedging a primary approach with a backup one, in an emergent manner that would be difficult to hand-design ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ). Compared to BoN, APR avoids redundant computation. APR models have control over what each parallel thread will do before branching out. Therefore, APR can learn to produce a set of unique, non-overlapping subtasks before assigning them to independent threads ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Stiennon et al., 2022 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ). Compared to non-adaptive approaches, APR can choose not to parallelize. Adaptive models can adjust the level of parallelization to match the complexity of the problem against the complexity and overhead of parallelization ( Lian et al., 2025 ). In practice, this is implemented by having the model output special tokens that control when to reason in parallel versus sequentially. Below is a condensed ThreadWeaver-style trace: two outlines and two paths under a <Parallel> block, then the threads agree on a single boxed answer. Figure 3: Example of an Adaptive Parallel Reasoning Trajectory from ThreadWeaver, manually condensed for ease of illustration. Figure 4: Special Tokens Variants across Adaptive Parallel Reasoning Papers Inference Systems for Adaptive Parallelism How do we actually execute parallel branches? We take inspiration from computer systems, and specifically, multithreading and multiprocessing. Most of this work can be viewed as leveraging a fork-join design. At inference time, we are effectively asking the model to perform a map-reduce operation: Fork the problem into subtasks/threads, process them concurrently Join them into a final answer Figure 5: Fork-join Inference Design Specifically, the model will encounter a list of subtasks. It will then prefill each of the subtasks and send them off as independent requests for the inference engine to process. These threads then decode concurrently until they hit an end token or exceed max length. This process blocks until all threads finish decoding and then aggregates the results. This is common across various adaptive parallel reasoning approaches. However, one issue arises during aggregation: the content generated in branches cannot be easily aggregated at the KV cache level. This is because tokens in independent threads start at identical position IDs, resulting in encoding overlap and non-standard behavior when merging KV cache back together. Similarly, since independent threads do not attend to each other, their concatenated KV cache results in a non-causal attention pattern, which the base model has not seen during training. To address this issue, the field splits into two schools of thought on how to execute the aggregation process, defined by whether they modify the inference engine or work around it. Multiverse modifies the inference engine to reuse KV cache across the join. Before taking a deeper look into Multiverse ( Yang et al., 2025 )'s memory management, let's first understand how KV cache is handled up until the "join" phase. Notice how each of the independent threads share the prefix sequence, i.e., the list of subtasks. Without optimization, each thread needs to prefill and recompute the KV cache for the prefix sequence. However, this redundancy can be avoided with SGLang 's RadixAttention ( Sheng et al., 2023 ), which organizes multiple requests into a radix tree, a trie (prefix tree) with sequences of elements of varying lengths instead of single elements. This way, the only new KV cache entries are those from independent thread generation. Figure 6: RadixAttention's KV Cache Management Strategy Now, if everything went well, all the independent threads have come back from the inference engine. Our goal is now to figure out how to synthesize them back into a single sequence to continue decoding for next steps. It turns out, we can reuse the KV cache of these independent threads during the synthesis stage. Specifically, Multiverse ( Yang et al., 2025 ), Parallel-R1 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ), and NPR ( Wu et al., 2025 ) modify the inference engine to copy over the KV cache generated by each thread and edits the page table so that it stitches together non-contiguous memory blocks into a single KV cache sequence. This avoids the redundant computation of a second prefill and reuses existing KV cache as much as possible. However, this has several major limitations. First, this approach requires modifying the inference engine to perform non-standard memory handling, which can result in unexpected behaviors. Specifically, since the synthesis request references KV cache from previous requests, it creates fragility in the system and the possibility of bad pointers. Another request can come in and evict the referenced KV cache before the synthesis request completes, requiring it to halt and trigger a re-prefilling of the previous thread request. This problem has led the Multiverse researchers ( Yang et al., 2025 ) to limit the batch size that the inference engine can handle, which restricts throughput. Figure 7: KV Cache "Stitching" During Multiverse Inference Second, this approach modifies how models see the sequence, which creates a distributional shift that models are not pretrained on, therefore requiring more extensive training to align behavior. Specifically, when we stitch together KV cache this way, we create a sequence with non-standard position encoding. During independent-thread generation, all threads started at the same position index and attended to the prior subtasks, NOT each other. So when the threads merge back, the resulting KV cache has a non-standard positional encoding and does not use causal attention. Therefore, this approach requires extensive training to align the model to this new behavior. To address this, Multiverse ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and related works apply a modified attention mask during training to prevent independent threads from attending to each other, aligning the training and inference behaviors. Figure 8: Multiverse's Attention Mask With these issues arising from non-standard KV cache management, can we try an approach without engine modifications? ThreadWeaver keeps the inference engine unchanged and moves orchestration to the client. ThreadWeaver ( Lian et al., 2025 ) treats parallel inference purely as a client-side problem. The "Fork" process is nearly identical to Multiverse's, but the join phase handles memory very differently as it does NOT modify engine internals. Instead, the client concatenates all text outputs from independent branches into one contiguous sequence. Then, the engine performs a second prefill to generate the KV cache for the conclusion generation step. While this introduces computational redundancy that Multiverse tries to avoid, the cost of prefill is significantly lower than decoding. In addition, this does not require special attention handling during inference, as the second prefill uses causal attention (threads see each other), making it easier to adapt sequential autoregressive models for this task. Figure 9: ThreadWeaver's Prefill and Decode Strategy How should we train a model to learn this behavior? Naively, for each parallel trajectory, we can break it down into multiple sequential pieces following our inference pattern. For instance, we would train the model to output the subtasks given prompt, individual threads given prompt+subtask assignment, and conclusion given prompt+subtasks+corresponding threads. However, this seems redundant and not compute efficient. Can we do better? Turns out, yes. As in ThreadWeaver ( Lian et al., 2025 ), we can organize a parallel trajectory into a prefix-tree (trie), flatten it into a single sequence, and apply an ancestor-only attention mask during training (not inference!). Figure 10: Building the Prefix-tree and Flattening into a single training sequence Specifically, we apply masking and position IDs to mimic the inference behavior, such that each thread is only conditioned on the prompt+subtasks, without ever attending to sibling threads or the final conclusion. The engine-agnostic design makes adoption easy since you don't need to figure out a separate hosting method and can leverage existing hardware infra. It also gets better as existing inference engines get better. What's more, with an engine-agnostic method, we can serve a hybrid model that switches between sequential and parallel thinking modes easily. Training Models to Use Parallelism Once the inference path exists, the next problem is teaching a model to use it. Demonstrations are needed because the model must learn to output special tokens that orchestrate control flow. We found the instruction-following capabilities of base models insufficient for generating parallel threads. An interesting question here is: does SFT training induce a fundamental reasoning capability for parallel execution that was previously absent, or does it merely align the model's existing pre-trained capabilities to a specific control-flow token syntax. Typical wisdom is SFT teaches new knowledge; but contrary to common belief, some papers—notably Parallel-R1 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) and NPR ( Wu et al., 2025 )—argue that their SFT demonstrations simply induce format following (i.e., how to structure parallel requests). We leave this as future work. Figure 11: Sources of Parallelization Demonstration Data Demonstrations teach the syntax of parallel control flow, but they do not fully solve the incentive problem. In an ideal world, we only need to reward the outcome accuracy, and the parallelization pattern emerges naturally given that it learns to output special tokens through SFT, similar to the emergence of long CoT. However, researchers ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) observed that this is not enough, and we do in fact need parallelization incentives. The question then becomes, how do we tell when the model is parallelizing effectively? Structure-only rewards are too easy to game. Naively, we can give a reward for the number of threads spawned. But models can spawn many short, useless threads to hack the reward. Okay, that doesn't work. How about a binary reward for simply using parallel structure correctly? This partially solves the issue of models spamming new threads, but models still learn to spawn threads when they don't need to. The authors of Parallel-R1 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) introduced an alternating-schedule, only rewarding parallel structure 20% of the time, which successfully increased the use of parallel structure (13.6% → 63%), but had little impact on overall accuracy. With this structure-only approach, we might be drifting away from our original goal of increasing accuracy and reducing latency… How can we optimize for the Pareto frontier directly? Accuracy is simple — we just look at the outcome. How about latency? Efficiency rewards need to track the critical path. In sequential-only trajectories, we can measure latency based on the total number of tokens generated. To extend this to parallel trajectories, we can focus on the critical path, or the longest sequence of tokens that are causally dependent, as this directly determines our end-to-end generation time (i.e., wall-clock time). As an example, when there are two <Parallel> sections with five threads each, the critical path will go through the longest thread from the first parallel section, then any sequential tokens, then the longest thread from the second parallel section, and so on until the end of sequence. Figure 12: Critical Path Length Illustration The goal is to minimize the length of the critical path. Simultaneously, we would still like the model to be spending tokens exploring threads in parallel. To combine the two objectives, we can focus on making the critical path a smaller fraction of the total tokens spent. Authors of ThreadWeaver ( Lian et al., 2025 ) framed the parallelization reward as $1 - L_{\mathrm{critical}} / L_{\mathrm{total}}$, which is 0 for a sequential trajectory, and increases linearly as the critical path gets smaller compared to the total tokens generated. Parallel efficiency should be gated by correctness. Intuitively, when multiple trajectories are correct we should assign more reward to the trajectories that are more efficient at parallelization. But how about when they are all incorrect? Should we assign any reward at all? Probably not. To formalize this, $R = R_{\mathrm{correctness}} + R_{\mathrm{parallel}}$. Assuming binary outcome correctness, this can be written as $R = \mathbf{1}(\text{Correctness}) + \mathbf{1}(\text{Correctness}) \times (\text{some parallelization metric})$. This way, a model only gets a parallelization reward when it answers correctly, since we don't want to pose parallelization constraints on the model if it couldn't answer the question correctly. Figure 13: Differences in Reward Designs Across Adaptive Parallel Reasoning Works Evaluation and Open Questions When all is said and done, how well do these adaptive parallel methods actually perform? Well…this is a hard question, as they differ in model choice and metrics. The model selection depends on the training method, SFT problem difficulty, and sequence length. When running SFT on difficult datasets like s1k, which contains graduate-level math and science problems, researchers chose a large base model (Qwen2.5 32B for Multiverse ( Yang et al., 2025 )) to capture the complex reasoning structure behind the solution trajectories. When running RL, researchers chose a small, non-CoT, instruct model (4B, 8B) due to compute cost constraints. Figure 14: Difference in Model Choice Across Adaptive Parallel Reasoning Papers Each paper also offers a slightly different interpretation about how adaptive parallel reasoning contributes to the research field. They optimize for different theoretical objectives, so they use slightly different sets of metrics: Multiverse and ThreadWeaver ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Lian et al., 2025 ) aim to deliver sequential-AR-model-level accuracy at faster speeds. Multiverse shows that APR models can achieve higher accuracy under the same fixed context window, while ThreadWeaver shows that the APR model achieves shorter end-to-end token latency (critical path length) while getting comparable accuracy. NPR ( Wu et al., 2025 ) treats sequential fallback as a failure mode and optimizes for 100% Genuine Parallelism Rate, measured as the ratio of parallel tokens to total tokens. Parallel-R1 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) does not focus on end-to-end latency and instead optimizes for exploration diversity, presenting APR as a form of mid-training exploration scaffold that provides a performance boost after RL. Open Questions While Adaptive Parallel Reasoning represents a promising step toward more efficient inference-time scaling, significant open questions remain. As noted above, Parallel-R1 ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) presents APR as a form of mid-training exploration scaffold rather than a primarily inference-time technique. This invites a more fundamental question: Does parallelization at inference-time consistently improve accuracy, or is it primarily valuable as a training-time exploration scaffold? Parallel-R1 suggests that the diversity induced by parallel structure during RL may matter more than the parallelization itself at test time. A related concern is stability. There's also a persistent tendency for models to collapse back to sequential reasoning when parallelization rewards are relaxed. Parallel-R1 authors showed that removing parallelization reward after 200 steps results in the model reverting to sequential behavior. Is this a training stability issue, a reward signal design issue, or evidence that parallel structure genuinely conflicts with how autoregressive pretraining shapes the model's prior? Beyond whether APR works, deployment introduces its own questions. Can we design training methods that account for available compute budget at inference time, so parallelization decisions are hardware-aware rather than purely problem-driven? Finally, the parallel structures considered above are essentially flat. What if we allow parallelization depth > 1? Recursive language models (RLMs; Zhang, Kraska and Khattab, 2026 ) effectively manage long context and show promising inference-time scaling capabilities. How well do RLMs perform when trained with end-to-end RL that incentivizes adaptive parallelization? Acknowledgements We thank Nicholas Tomlin and Alane Suhr for providing us with helpful feedback. We thank Christopher Park, Karl Vilhelmsson, Nyx Iskandar , Georgia Zhou, Kaival Shah , and Jyoti Rani for their insightful suggestions. We thank Vijay Kethana , Jaewon Chang , Cameron Jordan , Syrielle Montariol , Erran Li, and Anya Ji for their valuable discussions. We thank Jiayi Pan , Xiuyu Li , and Alex Zhang for their constructive correspondences about Adaptive Parallel Reasoning and Recursive Language Models.

items.title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
items.summary: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

items.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
items.summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

items.title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
items.summary: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.

items.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development
items.summary: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

items.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
items.summary: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

items.title: SpiderMark: Hybrid Watermarking for Generative AI via Algorithmic Injection and Learning-Based Verification
items.summary: The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has intensified the need for reliable methods to trace and verify the provenance of AI-generated images. Existing watermarking approaches for diffusion models typically rely on isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which are prone to directional vulnerability and threshold instability across diverse image transformations. We propose SpiderMark, a hybrid watermarking framework that combines algorithmic frequency-domain injection with learning-based probabilistic verification, requiring no modifications to pretrained diffusion model weights. SpiderMark embeds a structured spider-web pattern, comprising radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings, into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, and trains a lightweight ResNet-18 verifier augmented with auxiliary similarity cues (PSNR and L1) to produce a continuous watermark confidence score for watermark detection. Across nine evaluation conditions, SpiderMark achieves the highest fixed-threshold Accuracy in eight, while retaining strong detection on unseen COCO prompts without verifier retraining. CLIP similarity and FID measurements show that these detection gains are accompanied by small measured differences in prompt alignment and distributional image quality. SpiderMark establishes that structured watermark geometry and learned probabilistic verification can be unified into a single, practical framework, bridging the gap between imperceptibility, robustness, and real-world verifiability for generative AI content attribution.

items.title: Fuse to Recognize the Unseen: Class-Relative Infrared-Visible Fusion for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
items.summary: Visible-infrared image fusion leverages complementary thermal cues to enhance visual perception, particularly under challenging illumination. However, such perceptual complementarity does not readily translate into semantic gains in open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS), where CLIP-based models are predominantly pretrained on RGB imagery. Directly introducing IR information may instead disrupt RGB-language alignment, turning promising thermal cues into semantic interference that undermines unseen-class recognition. Our pixel-level RGB-IR semantic analysis reveals that class-relevant thermal cues can correct certain RGB misclassifications while preserving reliable RGB predictions, motivating RGB-anchored, class-relative thermal cue selection. Based on this insight, we propose EmergeFuse, an infrared-visible fusion framework for OVSS that selectively converts complementary thermal evidence into unseen-class semantic corrections. Specifically, class-relative cue selection evaluates RGB-IR semantic responses and calibrated thermal evidence relative to RGB predictions, generating class-relative correction requests through competitive selection. Text-contrast image rectification then translates these selected requests into semantic rectification directions through text contrasts, guiding evidence-gated feature updates to realize complementary thermal evidence for unseen-class recognition. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate gains of up to 4.755% in unseen-class mIoU and 15.730% in strict complementary conversion rate over existing fusion methods, while maintaining competitive fusion quality.

items.title: Adaptive Action Horizon Selection via Flow-Field Uncertainty
items.summary: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.

items.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
items.summary: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

items.title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
items.summary: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

items.title: TapTacTouch: Shape Completion from Sparse Tactile Contacts with Geometric Priors
items.summary: 3D object reconstruction is essential for robotic perception and manipulation, yet conventional approaches predominantly rely on visual observations that can be limited by occlusion or unavailable in visually constrained environments. In this work, we propose a vision-free, training-free, and category-agnostic framework for reconstructing 3D object meshes from sparse tactile contacts without relying on pretrained shape models. A 6-DoF robotic arm equipped with a 20-DoF multi-finger robotic hand collects tactile observations using 3x3 pressure sensor arrays mounted on the finger pads. The acquired tactile measurements are transformed into 3D contact constraints through robot kinematics and integrated into a multi-scale Gaussian Process Implicit Surface (GPIS). To address sparse and incomplete surface observations, the proposed method incorporates contact confidence weighting, weak pseudo-surface constraints, and an observation-driven geometric prior to preserve local surface geometry and provide structural guidance in unobserved regions. Real-world experiments on six objects achieve a Chamfer Distance (CD) of 1.610, an Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) of 7.738, and an F-Score of 95.00, with reconstruction completed in an average of 49.99 s per object. These results demonstrate that sparse tactile sensing can provide sufficient geometric information for continuous 3D object reconstruction without visual or semantic information.

items.title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
items.summary: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies correctly, so that the circuit imitates the teacher where the teacher is right. On TweetEval-emotion, the complete circuit of DistilGPT2 reaches a test gold accuracy of 66.5 $\pm$ 1.3% with order selection and 57.4 $\pm$ 2.5% with rule selection over three seeds, against 74.7% for the teacher and 64.0% for a bag of word pieces fitted on the same tweets, and that of BERT-base reaches 70.0 $\pm$ 0.5% with order selection and 63.7 $\pm$ 1.2% with rule selection against 77.8%. The circuit needs no multiplier and no weight traffic, and its exported hardware description reproduces it bit for bit. By a synthesis-based estimate it classifies one tweet in about 1-2 $μ$s (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 $μ$s (BERT) on an FPGA card and in 5-9 $μ$s on a palm-sized board whose module draws 7.5-15 W, two to three orders of magnitude faster than the network on a GPU at batch 1 (measured, 0.9-2.6 ms for DistilGPT2 including an optimised CUDA-graph baseline), at a cost of 8.5 (DistilGPT2) and 8.6 (BERT) points of gold accuracy for the synthesised seed-0 circuits.

items.title: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-TRESS.

items.title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

items.title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

items.title: Towards Fair Resource Sharing in Agentic LLM Serving
items.summary: As LLM agents increasingly execute complex, multi-step tasks on shared inference infrastructure, resource contention across the end-to-end LLM serving stack causes severe and uneven slowdowns across agents. Existing agentic serving systems primarily optimize throughput and latency, with comparatively limited attention to fairness among concurrent agents. Although fairness has been studied in conventional LLM serving at the token and request levels, these approaches do not fully capture cumulative delays and stateful resource dependencies across successive LLM calls within an agent. Moreover, interference spans request routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware resources, making agent-level fairness challenging to define and optimize across an end-to-end serving stack. This paper presents a cross-layer framework to define agent-level fairness, attribute sources of unfairness, and optimize fairness while preserving throughput. To account for agents with widely varying execution demands, we build a theoretical foundation to define fairness using slowdown relative to standalone execution. Our empirical analysis reveals that routing, runtime scheduling, and hardware contention jointly determine fairness, with performance-oriented policies often leading to prolonged queuing delays. To optimize fairness, we introduce Duru, which monitors each agent's slowdown and uses this signal to guide admission and scheduling decisions across the router and runtime. Duru further alleviates starvation through admission exceptions and integrates slowdown-driven autoscaling to adhere to Service-Level Objectives (SLOs). Our evaluation across various benchmarks and hardware platforms shows that Duru reduces 99th-percentile normalized slowdown by a geometric mean of 44.4% (up to 79.5%) while delivering 91.8-127.4% of the state-of-the-art system's throughput.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
items.summary: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. Yet even without sufficient data, domain experts often know which physics the LF model omits and under which conditions its effect grows. Existing multi-fidelity (MF) models cannot use such qualitative knowledge directly, but large language models (LLMs) can interpret it and compare designs accordingly. The proposed LLM-Assisted MFBO adds a knowledge basis to the conventional MF model: from an expert description of the omitted physics, an LLM judges which of two designs requires the larger signed residual correction, and a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into the basis. HF data calibrate its contribution and sign, so the knowledge is not trusted blindly. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, the proposed method reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. Knowledge quality, rather than the choice of LLM, determined whether the search was accelerated, as shown by a controlled study that varied the two independently. A knowledge-level ablation further quantified the contribution of each knowledge statement. These results show that LLM-interpreted expert knowledge can complement numerical data as an information source in MFBO.

items.title: Asymmetric Decomposition for Multi-Agent Path Finding with Unassigned Agents
items.summary: Robots without assigned tasks may obstruct active robots, while routing them to designated parking locations can cause unnecessary travel. This article proposes flow-oracle conflict-based search (FOCBS) for Multi-Agent Path Finding with unassigned agents (MAPF-UA). FOCBS searches over assigned-agent paths using conflict-based search (CBS) and routes targetless unassigned agents through a min-cost flow oracle. When the selected assigned-agent paths leave unassigned agents no collision-free paths, flow-conflict branching converts min-cut blockers into assigned-agent constraints, which guide the search without excluding optimal solutions. A batched zero-cost warm start accelerates the oracle, and start-avoiding tie-breaking reduces unassigned-agent movement. For feasible instances on finite graphs, we prove termination and global minimization of assigned-agent sum of service time, measured by last-arrival times. Unassigned-agent movement is minimized conditional on the selected assigned-agent paths, without a global lexicographic optimality guarantee. Benchmark experiments show that FOCBS scales well with the number of unassigned agents, and ablation studies show that, compared with discarding non-completable assigned-agent paths, flow-conflict branching solves substantially more instances while retaining optimality. Simulation and physical-robot experiments demonstrate plan executability, with laboratory tests reducing fleet travel by 40.8% relative to the parking-based coordination baseline. The source code and related resources are available at https://github.com/Chin-hsi/focbs

items.title: BEV-Diffusion: Camera-Only Traversability Navigation with BEV Memory and Efficient Cross-Robot Adaptation
items.summary: Robot navigation requires both an understanding of the scene and an efficient adaptation to new robots, yet current methods rely on expensive LiDAR sensors, long mapping and modular pipelines. We present BEV-Diffusion, a camera-only model that learns a bird's-eye view (BEV) traversability map, its uncertainty and the path in a single network. A frozen DINOv2 backbone encodes consecutive RGB frames, which inverse perspective mapping and Bayesian fusion lift into the BEV, and a ranking loss keeps outdoor traversability graded rather than binary, separating asphalt from grass (median 0.94 vs. 0.75). On this map, a transformer denoiser generates polar waypoints in a few DDIM steps, and uncertainty-aware guidance refines the path and ends it where the map is no longer reliable. At deployment, a metric BEV memory keeps obstacles after they leave the camera view and warm starts each sample from the previous, ego-motion compensated path. Because the planner jointly learns the path, the map, and its uncertainty, it selects routes through terrain it can confidently traverse. In an unseen courtyard, a wheeled-legged robot autonomously traveled 120 m, completing 96% of the route without intervention, compared with 75-88% for the baselines. Even under low-light conditions after sunset, the proposed model completed the route without requiring any intervention. Retraining only the BEV head, about 3% of the parameters, adapts the model to a small legged robot in 2.3 min. Indoors, the memory gets this robot out of maze-like traps: it retains 62-66% of the nearby out-of-view obstacles, against at most 3% for the baselines, and the robot achieves 67-100% task progress, compared with 20-40% for the evaluated baselines.

items.title: Can Weight-Space Programming Alter Learned Ethical Priorities?
items.summary: We investigate whether a weight edit can alter how a model trades off honoring a commitment against benefiting more people. In a concept-supervised text model, we alter fitted choice weights so that the benefit required to override a formal pledge is larger than for an ordinary promise. Across six independently trained text readers, the edit selects the larger group in both orders on 100% of targeted ordinary conflicts and 83.3% of targeted formal conflicts. It preserves the source model's success rates on smaller conflicts and its factual accuracy. The remaining formal-conflict failures coincide with errors reading a beneficiary number. A separate classifier demonstrates why this distinction matters: reusing a factual answer passes an unconditional choice test but fails to preserve small-gap promises. In a YOLO11n pilot on COCO128, a bias edit increased small-target matches from 3/43 to 9/43, and an equivalent score calibration reproduced the retained detections. These exploratory results show a way to test selective changes to learned priorities in a model with an exposed trade-off mechanism. Whether the method can discover such changes in less structured language models remains open.

items.title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
items.summary: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

items.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
items.summary: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

items.title: Giving robots a better feel for object manipulation
items.summary: Giving robots a better feel for object manipulation rachelg Mon, 04/29/2019 - 13:27 Video April 29 '19 Rob Matheson Model improves a robot's ability to mold materials into shapes and interact with liquids and solid objects. A new learning system developed by MIT researchers improves robots' abilities to mold materials into target shapes and make predictions about interacting with solid objects and liquids. The system, known as a learning-based particle simulator, could give industrial robots a more refined touch — and it may have fun applications in personal robotics, such as modelling clay shapes or rolling sticky rice for sushi. In robotic planning, physical simulators are models that capture how different materials respond to force. Robots are "trained" using the models, to predict the outcomes of their interactions with objects, such as pushing a solid box or poking deformable clay. But traditional learning-based simulators mainly focus on rigid objects and are unable to handle fluids or softer objects. Some more accurate physics-based simulators can handle diverse materials, but rely heavily on approximation techniques that introduce errors when robots interact with objects in the real world. In a paper being presented at the International Conference on Learning Representations in May, the researchers describe a new model that learns to capture how small portions of different materials — "particles" — interact when they're poked and prodded. The model directly learns from data in cases where the underlying physics of the movements are uncertain or unknown. Robots can then use the model as a guide to predict how liquids, as well as rigid and deformable materials, will react to the force of its touch. As the robot handles the objects, the model also helps to further refine the robot's control. In experiments, a robotic hand with two fingers, called "RiceGrip," accurately shaped a deformable foam to a desired configuration — such as a "T" shape — that serves as a proxy for sushi rice. In short, the researchers' model serves as a type of "intuitive physics" brain that robots can leverage to reconstruct three-dimensional objects somewhat similarly to how humans do. " Humans have an intuitive physics model in our heads, where we can imagine how an object will behave if we push or squeeze it. Based on this intuitive model, humans can accomplish amazing manipulation tasks that are far beyond the reach of current robots," says first author Yunzhu Li, a graduate student in the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). " We want to build this type of intuitive model for robots to enable them to do what humans can do." "When children are 5 months old, they already have different expectations for solids and liquids," adds co-author Jiajun Wu, a CSAIL graduate student. "That's something we know at an early age, so maybe that's something we should try to model for robots." Joining Li and Wu on the paper are: Russ Tedrake, a CSAIL researcher and a professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS); Joshua Tenenbaum, a professor in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and a member of CSAIL and the Center for Brains, Minds, and Machines (CBMM); and Antonio Torralba, a professor in EECS and director of the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab. Dynamic graphs A key innovation behind the model, called the "particle interaction network" (DPI-Nets), was creating dynamic interaction graphs, which consist of thousands of nodes and edges that can capture complex behaviors of so-called particles. In the graphs, each node represents a particle. Neighboring nodes are connected with each other using directed edges, which represent the interaction passing from one particle to the other. In the simulator, particles are hundreds of small spheres combined to make up some liquid or a deformable object. The graphs are constructed as the basis for a machine-learning system called a graph neural network. In training, the model over time learns how particles in different materials react and reshape. It does so by implicitly calculating various properties for each particle — such as its mass and elasticity — to predict if and where the particle will move in the graph when perturbed. The model then leverages a "propagation" technique, which instantaneously spreads a signal throughout the graph. The researchers customized the technique for each type of material — rigid, deformable, and liquid — to shoot a signal that predicts particles positions at certain incremental time steps. At each step, it moves and reconnects particles, if needed. For example, if a solid box is pushed, perturbed particles will be moved forward. Because all particles inside the box are rigidly connected with each other, every other particle in the object moves the same calculated distance, rotation, and any other dimension. Particle connections remain intact and the box moves as a single unit. But if an area of deformable foam is indented, the effect will be different. Perturbed particles move forward a lot, surrounding particles move forward only slightly, and particles farther away won't move at all. With liquids being sloshed around in a cup, particles may completely jump from one end of the graph to the other. The graph must learn to predict where and how much all affected particles move, which is computationally complex. Shaping and adapting In their paper, the researchers demonstrate the model by tasking the two-fingered RiceGrip robot with clamping target shapes out of deformable foam. The robot first uses a depth-sensing camera and object-recognition techniques to identify the foam. The researchers randomly select particles inside the perceived shape to initialize the position of the particles. Then, the model adds edges between particles and reconstructs the foam into a dynamic graph customized for deformable materials. Because of the learned simulations, the robot already has a good idea of how each touch, given a certain amount of force, will affect each of the particles in the graph. As the robot starts indenting the foam, it iteratively matches the real-world position of the particles to the targeted position of the particles. Whenever the particles don't align, it sends an error signal to the model. That signal tweaks the model to better match the real-world physics of the material. Next, the researchers aim to improve the model to help robots better predict interactions with partially observable scenarios, such as knowing how a pile of boxes will move when pushed, even if only the boxes at the surface are visible and most of the other boxes are hidden. The researchers are also exploring ways to combine the model with an end-to-end perception module by operating directly on images. This will be a joint project with Dan Yamins's group; Yamin recently completed his postdoc at MIT and is now an assistant professor at Stanford University. "You're dealing with these cases all the time where there's only partial information," Wu says. "We're extending our model to learn the dynamics of all particles, while only seeing a small portion."

items.title: eFAIR: Fair LLM Serving under Hourly Electricity Commitments
items.summary: Datacenters can procure electricity in day-ahead markets by committing to energy purchases for individual hours. For LLM services operating within these hourly budgets, maximizing aggregate throughput alone may still leave individual requests waiting or receiving much slower service than desired. Fair serving therefore requires improving service for poorly served requests while reserving electricity for later arrivals whose timing and demand are unknown. To compare service across requests, we define normalized throughput as each request's actual output rate divided by the product of its standalone throughput and its service entitlement, a positive weight representing its desired service level. Using this measure, we formulate fair serving as leximin optimization under an hourly electricity constraint, prioritizing requests with the lowest normalized throughput. To address this problem, we present eFAIR, an online scheduler that coordinates request dispatching, electricity budget allocation, and GPU frequency selection through a common normalized-throughput target. Specifically, request dispatching prioritizes requests by desired service level and progress; electricity budget allocation reserves electricity for current and expected future work; and frequency selection uses electricity savings to raise GPU frequencies for requests with higher desired service levels. Evaluations on H20 and H200 configurations, each with 32 replicas, show that eFAIR improves the tenth percentile of normalized throughput by 28.0%-31.0% over the best budget-feasible baseline, while keeping absolute deviations from the hourly electricity commitment below 0.26%. eFAIR also improves throughput balance among concurrent requests and aligns electricity allocation more closely with service demand over time. Together, these results demonstrate how eFAIR improves request-level fairness within an hourly commitment.

items.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
items.summary: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

items.title: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning
items.summary: The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/UEC-InabaLab/CounselTraj.
